source.title: Assessing and Learning Alignment of Unimodal Vision and Language Models
source.authors: Le Zhang; Qian Yang; Aishwarya Agrawal

record.tranche_reason: The study measures cross-modal alignment with a learned linear alignment probe and zero-shot retrieval, rather than the original sources' measures. It varies pretrained model families and capability and reports alignment results.
record.gate_note: Part I directly tests alignment potential: it freezes unimodal encoders, learns linear alignment layers from CC3M image-text pairs, and evaluates COCO retrieval. Exact per-model retrieval values are presented in figures, not transcribed in the text. Part II's SAIL results are excluded as evidence of pre-existing alignment because that training intentionally learns alignment. Related-work claims are not results of this study.
record.test_reason: Part I freezes unimodal vision and language encoders and fits linear alignment layers on CC3M pairs. It scores COCO zero-shot retrieval (R@10) while sweeping vision models against a GTE language anchor and language models against a DINOv2-L vision anchor. It relates alignment to model size and capability (k-NN, linear probe, MTEB). This is a different method aimed at whether cross-modal alignment grows with capability, so T2. Part II (SAIL) trains alignment on purpose and is not evidence on pre-existing convergence.
record.authors_conclusion: Broadly correct. The authors conclude that unimodal vision and language models show strong inherent alignment, 50–75% R@10 for most models, consistent with Huh et al. Alignment depends on the SSL objective and above all on clustering quality (k-NN) rather than linear separability. Stronger language models align better and matter for complex reasoning. These findings motivate SAIL, which learns alignment efficiently.
record.recipe_differences: The study proposes alignment probing: it fits linear layers on paired image-text data and evaluates COCO retrieval, rather than reproducing the original sources' representation-similarity measurements.
record.method_sensitivity: Alignment performance varies with the vision model's SSL objective and representation clustering quality; MAE is weaker, while larger models and higher-capability language models are reported to align better.
record.problems: Per-model alignment values in Figure 2 are not transcribed as text. The alignment score is obtained after fitting a linear layer on paired data, so it measures alignment potential under that procedure rather than unmodified cross-modal distances. The reported trend varies by model family and anchor; no uncertainty estimates are given for the alignment results.
record.rows_left_out: Excluded Part II SAIL downstream-task results, including classification, retrieval, segmentation and LLaVA evaluations, because they follow deliberate alignment training and do not independently measure pre-existing alignment. Also excluded cited prior-study results and general comparisons that do not report an outcome for the alignment object itself.

untested.parts: Only cross-modal pairs with one model fixed. No same-modality convergence and no joint scaling of both models. Alignment is measured only after fitting a map on paired data, not as intrinsic similarity.
Both modalities are never scaled together. Alignment is measured as retrieval after a trained linear map, not as kernel or nearest-neighbour similarity of the frozen representations.
Only paired-data linear layers into a shared space. No stitching, no relative representations, no unpaired mapping.
The alignment metric and evaluation data are not varied. The k-NN vs linear-probe comparison concerns the capability measure, not the similarity measure.
Retrieval of 50–75% R@10 shows alignment is incomplete, but there is no test of plateau or of shared-data explanations.

missing.what: General statement that within families larger vision models consistently give better alignment. The V1/V2 scale verdicts rest on it, but no aggregate row records it.
CLIP-L reference alignment score of 80.1% under the same probe, as a baseline row. Also gte-small reaching 80% of CLIP with 30% of its text-encoder parameters.
Fig. 8: MAE is an outlier, with high linear-probe accuracy but low alignment.

record.verdict_notes: Not an original source. Most per-model values are figure only, so the scale verdicts lean on the authors' prose and the aggregate correlations. Correlations come from a small number of models with no uncertainty reported. The appendix says alignment probing used sigmoid loss, ShareGPT4-enhanced captions and multi-positive contrast, which differs from the main text's plain contrastive linear probe. The 'alignment potential' measured therefore depends on that training recipe.

versions.untested_parts: The study varies one modality at a time against a fixed anchor; it does not test both models scaling jointly, or establish a general trend across all architectures, objectives, data and modalities.

Tests image-caption alignment potential after fitting a linear map with paired data, varying vision or language models separately against a fixed anchor; it does not test a joint scale sweep of both modalities.
Only paired-data-trained linear alignment layers are assessed. The study does not test stitching, relative representations, or mapping without paired data.
The alignment metric and evaluation dataset are not varied; comparisons of k-NN and linear probing concern predictors of alignment, not alternative alignment measures or input distributions.

The study notes that alignment varies with SSL objective, but does not test whether shared training data or objectives explain alignment instead of a common model of reality, or whether alignment plateaus.
